result.summary: Apollodorus lists the children of Deucalion, then tells how Minos's young son Glaucus drowned in a honey jar. The seer Polyidus finds and revives him using a herb a serpent used, but Minos forces him to teach Glaucus divination, and Polyidus makes him forget it.

scenes.title: Deucalion's children; Glaucus drowns
scenes.summary: Deucalion's children are listed. The child Glaucus chases a mouse and drowns in a jar of honey.
scenes.stakes: Glaucus's life, lost in a childhood accident.

scenes.title: Polyidus finds and revives Glaucus
scenes.summary: Minos searches for Glaucus and the diviners, led by Polyidus, find him. Shut in with the corpse, Polyidus learns of a resurrecting herb from a serpent and revives the boy.
scenes.stakes: Polyidus's life, since Minos demands the boy back alive.

scenes.title: Forgotten divination
scenes.summary: Minos makes Polyidus teach Glaucus divination before leaving for Argos. Polyidus has Glaucus spit into his mouth, and the boy forgets the art.
scenes.stakes: Polyidus's freedom to return home to Argos.

notable_quotes.reason: Memorable ending: Glaucus loses his divination by spitting, undoing Minos's forced lesson.

analysis.text: The tale shows the limits of royal power: Minos can compel a seer to act but cannot keep what is taught under compulsion.
Death and revival through a serpent's herb connects to wider Greek ideas of serpents as healers.

legacy.text: The story of Polyidus and Glaucus was dramatized in lost tragedies, including one by Euripides.

fun_facts.text: The footnote numbers show this is a translation with notes, likely J. G. Frazer's 1921 edition.

language_notes.text: "Bastard" here simply means a son born outside marriage; it carries no insult in this context.
The Curetes were divine attendants associated with Crete and the infant Zeus; here they act as prophets. The riddle of the three-colored cow is the oracle's clue.
"Compared the color of the cow to the fruit of the bramble": the blackberry changes color as it ripens (white, red, black), matching the cow's three colors.
"He was shut up with the dead body": Minos imprisons Polyidus in a tomb with the corpse until he succeeds.
Argos was Polyidus' home, so Minos is keeping him from returning there.
Europa, a Phoenician princess carried to Crete by Jove, was mother of Minos; this closes the account of her descendants.

context_notes.text: Minos was the legendary king of Crete, known for his power and later as a judge of the dead.
Polyidus was a seer from Argos, famed for interpreting signs and omens.
Spitting was thought to pass or remove power, so the spittle transfers or cancels the seer's knowledge.

literary_notes.text: A child's playful chase ends in a sweet, absurd death, a grim contrast with the sweetness of honey.
The second serpent's herb mirrors what Polyidus will do, so the animal's act prefigures and teaches the human one.
The restoration of knowledge so hard won ends abruptly in a flat, ironic reversal: Minos's compulsion is undone by a trick.
